     II.  MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT                                   
12

14                                                                       
        A.  Legal Standard                                              
15                                                                       
        Summary  judgment  is  appropriate  when  the  pleadings,  depositions,  answers  to 
16                                                                       
   interrogatories, and admissions on file, together with the affidavits, if any, show “that there is no 
17                                                                       
   genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” 
18                                                                       
   Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a); accord Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322 (1986). The substantive 
19                                                                       
   law governing a matter determines which facts are material to a case. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, 
20                                                                       
   477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). The moving party bears the burden of showing the absence of material 
21                                                                       
   fact. Celotex, 477 U.S. at 323. The burden then shifts to the nonmoving party to show specific 
22                                                                       
   facts demonstrating a genuine factual dispute for trial. See Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith 
23                                                                       
   Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574, 587 (1986). When considering the propriety of summary judgment, 
24                                                                       
   the court views all facts and draws all inferences in the light most favorable to the nonmoving 
25                                                                       
   party. Gonzalez v. City of Anaheim, 747 F.3d 789, 793 (9th Cir. 2014). 
26                                                                       
        However, the nonmoving party may not merely rest on the allegations of their pleadings. 
27                                                                       
   They must produce specific facts by affidavit or other evidence showing a genuine issue of fact. 
28                                                                       
   Anderson, 477 U.S. at 256. In other words, the nonmoving party “must do more than simply show 
1   that there is some metaphysical doubt as to the material facts . . . . Where the record taken as a 
2   whole could not lead a rational trier of fact to find for the nonmoving party, there is no genuine 
3   issue for trial.” Scott v. Harris, 550 U.S. 372, 380 (2007) (alteration in original) (internal quotation 
4   marks omitted). It is improper for the Court to resolve genuine factual disputes or make credibility 
5   determinations at the summary judgment stage. Zetwick v. Cty. of Yolo, 850 F.3d 436, 441 (9th 
6   Cir. 2017) (citations omitted).                                      
7        B.  Incorporation of Findings of the Class Certification Order  
8        The Court now turns to determining whether there is “no genuine issue of material fact.” 
9   Anderson, 477 U.S. at 247–48 (emphasis original). For the reasons below, the Court finds that 
10  based upon the record and its prior findings there are genuine issues of disputed fact in the case 
11  requiring a trial on the merits.                                     
12       First, the Court finds that its Certification Order reviewed relevant admissible evidence and 
13  considered the substantive issues in dispute in the Defendant’s Motion for Summary Judgment. 
14  Specifically, the remaining disputed class action claims are alleged violations of Section 2 of the 
15  Sherman Antitrust Act. 15 U.S.C. § 2. The elements of a claim for such antitrust action are: (1) the 
16  existence of an antitrust violation; (2) “antitrust injury” or “impact” flowing from that violation; 
17  and (3) measurable damages. See Big Bear Lodging Ass’n v. Snow Summit Inc., 182 F.3d 1096, 
18  1101–02 (9th Cir. 1999); In re Hydrogen Peroxide Antitrust Litig., 552 F.3d 305, 311 (3d Cir. 
19  2008), as amended (Jan. 16, 2009). Plaintiffs’ claim is that Zuffa violated Section 2 based on its 
20  alleged monopsony power, that is, where a single buyer has concentrated power on the buyer side 
21  of the market.2 To show a violation of antitrust law here, Plaintiffs must show Zuffa (1) possessed 
22  monopsony power in the relevant markets, (2) willfully acquired or maintained its monopsony 
23  power through exclusionary conduct, and (3) caused antitrust injury through such conduct. Am. 
24  Pro. Testing Serv. Inc. v. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich Legal & Pro. Publ’ns, Inc., 108 F.3d 1147, 
25

10  common application of that scheme led to common or similar injury among the class, and (4) that 
11  there are measurable monetary damages proven by common evidence which arise from the 
12  anticompetitive conduct and not procompetative conduct.”).           
13       Second, the Court finds that the relevant and admissible evidence it must now review and 
14  consider on summary judgement is duplicative of the evidence that it reviewed for its Certification 
15  Order, that the standard at certification was in fact higher than for summary judgement, and that, 
16  therefore, its reasoning and findings in its Certification Order would and do apply with equal force 
17  to Defendant’s Motion for Summary Judgment.                          
18       A party seeking to certify a class under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23 bears the burden 
19  of showing that they have satisfied “[T]he burden of establishing that the prerequisites of Rule 23 
20  [is] satisfied by a preponderance of the evidence.” Olean, 31 F.4th at 665 (joining sister circuits in 
21  this conclusion). Where, as here, the class is based on proving a common question predominates, 
22  “[c]onsidering whether ‘questions of law or fact common to class members predominate’ begins, 
23  of course, with the elements of the underlying cause of action.’” Id. (quoting Erica P. John Fund, 
24  Inc. v. Halliburton Co., 563 U.S. 804, 809 (2011) (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3))). A district 
25  court must engage in a “rigorous analysis,” often requiring some evaluation of the “merits of the 
26  plaintiff’s underlying claim,” before finding that the prerequisites for certification have been 
27  satisfied. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338, 350 (2011); see also Comcast Corp. v. 
28  Behrend, 569 U.S. 27, 33-34 (2013). Moreover, and importantly, the standard at certification—
1   preponderance—is, in antitrust cases like this one, more exacting than the standard at summary 
2   judgment which requires only a genuine issue of disputed fact. This is especially the case here 
3   where a district court must (and did) weigh and resolve fundamental disputes between the parties’ 
4   experts. Olean, 61 F.4th at 666 (holding that class certification includes “weighing conflicting 
5   expert testimony” and “resolving expert disputes”) (internal citations omitted). 
6        The Court finds that the evidence submitted for both class certification and summary 
7   judgement is overlapping and admissible. Only admissible evidence can be considered in a ruling 
8   on summary judgment. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(e); Orr v. Bank of Am., 285 F.3d 764, 773 (9th Cir. 
9   2002). Evidence must be authenticated or presented in a form that would be otherwise admissible 
10  at trial. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(2); id., advisory comm. note to 2010 amendments (“The burden 
11  is on the proponent to show that the material is admissible as presented or to explain the admissible 
12  form that is anticipated.”); Fed. R. Evid. 901(a); see also Fraser v. Goodale, 342 F.3d 1032, 1037 
13  (9th Cir. 2003) (“Because the diary's contents could be presented in an admissible form at trial, we 
14  may consider the diary's contents in the Bank's summary judgment motion.”). To be considered, 
15  expert declarations must be properly disclosed or the proponent of the evidence must show the 
16  failure was substantially justified or harmless. Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1); Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a) 
17  (outlining disclosure requirements). “Expert opinion is admissible and may defeat summary 
18  judgment if it appears the affiant is competent to give an expert opinion and the factual basis for 
19  the opinion is stated in the affidavit, even though the underlying factual details and reasoning upon 
20  which the opinion is based are not.” Walton v. U.S. Marshals Serv., 492 F.3d 998, 1008 (9th Cir. 
21  2007) (quoting Bulthuis v. Rexal Corp., 789 F.2d 1315, 1318 (9th Cir. 1985) (per curiam)); Rebel 
22  Oil, 51 F.3d at 1435. In the context of class certification, evidence must also be admissible. Olean, 
23  31 F.4th at 665 (citing Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Bouaphakeo, 577 U.S. 442, 454–55 (9th Cir. 2016). 
24  The Court finds that the evidence it considered at class certification, including the written expert 
25  reports, sworn expert/witness testimony during certification and other documentary evidence, is 
26  both admissible and relevant for the purposes of summary judgment.3 Significantly, the Order on 
27  Class Certification considered and found admissible the opinions of Dr. Singer and Dr. Zimbalist

4        The Court next reviews Zuffa’s arguments for summary judgment and finds that, based
